newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: PRESS DIGEST-Australian General News - April 11.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST-Australian General News - April 11.

text.p: (Compiled for Reuters by Media Monitors)
THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW

Seasonally adjusted unemployment figures released by the Australian Bureau of Statistics yesterday indicate unemployment increased by 33,900 during March. The Federal Government responded to the figures with an extra A$22 million commitment to double the number of apprenticeships and trainees in small business to 40,000 over the next three years. Page 1.

Embattled Senator Mal Colston was admitted to a Brisbane hospital last night as a pressure on him to stand down as Senate Deputy President mounted and rorting allegations continued. A hospital spokesperson said the Senator had been admitted for a "medical condition and he is resting comfortably". Page 4.

Federal Health Minister Michael Wooldridge yesterday unveiled a package of reforms for the private health insurance industry as part of the Government's response to the Productivity Commission's review of private health insurance. The health insurance indstry welcomed the reforms, saying they would usher in a new dynamic market, increase competition, boost ailing membership, and lead to lower premiums for consumers. Page 5.
THE AUSTRALIAN

In a major overhaul of the health insurance industry the Federal Government proposes to enforce people over 30 joining a health fund to pay higher premiums, giving insurers a virtual free hand to increase charges. The Government is also considering allowing the funds to refuse membership to people over 25 who are already sick. The package of reforms, designed to stop the decline in fund membership, will also try to alleviate "hit and run" claimants by extending waiting periods for benefits. Page 1.

China has placed support behind a human rights dialogue with Australia, proposed by the Prime Minister John Howard as Australia withdrew from a United Nations resolution condemning China's human rights records. China has given "in principle" agreement to he Australian proposal which is scheduled to start this year. Page 1.

Western Australian has introduced a controversial gold tax as the Court Government handed down its Budget yesterday. The move has brought widespread criticism from key players in the State's mining industry and has broken a major election commitment. The budget also saw moderate increases in a range of consumer charges including gas, electricity and car registrations. Page 1.

It has been revealed that Fraser Government Administrative Services Minister Kevin Newman made an application for Federal police to investigate embattled Senator Mal Colston as early as 1982. Newman decided against the move when his department advised that there was not enough evidence to carry out a police investigation into alleged travel rorts by Colston. Page 3.
THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD

Under Federal Government moves to reverse the decline in the private health insurance industry, a range of recommendations will see older people being penalised for not taking out private health insurance and younger people may see a lifetime's worth of cheaper premiums. The changes were outlined in a Productivity Commission report which also advocated strategies to reduce the incidence of "hit and run" private health cover. Page 1.

The Federal Government has softened its views on human-rights abuses by refusing to support a UN resolution condemning China for its record on human rights. This is the first time Australia has withdrawn support for the resolution since the Tiananmen Squae massacre six years ago. In a move designed to ease diplomatic tension, Canberra intends to entice Beijing to hold regular talks on the issue of human rights. Page 1.

Major insurer NRMA plans to muscle in on Sydney's car dealers by spending up to A$43 million to build Australia's biggest and most "customer-friendly" used car yard in the city's inner west. The plan has received immediate criticism from dealers who claim it could put up to 600 operators out of business. Page 1.

The bodies of two women were discovered in calm seas off the Kiama Blowhole, a popular tourist attraction south of Wollongong. There are no witnesses to the deaths and police remain unsure if the two were swept off the rocks near the blowhole, fell into the hole or floated there from another location. The deaths follow seven people being swept off the blowhole rocks by a freak wave five years ago. Page 3.
THE AGE

In a Federal Government bid to revive the private health system, older people who join private funds will be penalised with higher premiums. The Productivity Commission final report into the private health industry also called for penalties imposed on indviduals who are seen to abuse the system by taking out short-term fund membership to cover the cost of one-off treatment. Page A1.

Victorian Auditor-General Ches Baragwanath has clashed with the State Government over a number of civic projects. In a report to Parliament, Baragwanath says the Government did not conduct a feasibility study into the State Library redevelopment, the Reget Theatre refurbishment and the construction of the Melbourne Exhibition Centre - projects worth almost A$400 million in total. Page A1.

The Federal Government has softened its views on human-rights abuses by refusing to support a United Nations resolution condemning China for its human rights record. This is the first time Australia has withdrawn support for the resolution since the Tianamen Square massacre six years ago. Page A1.

Retiring Victorian Supreme Court Judge Justice Alec Southwell has reaffirmed his controversial 1991 ruling that upheld a judgement that raping a prostitute was less of a crime than raping a "chaste" women. On the eve of his retirement, Australia's longest serving judge conceded he did not know whether the judiciary was "out-of-touch" with community attitudes. Page A1.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
